nameStory: The 'speedwell' name comes from an old English farewell blessing meaning 'may you speed well' or have a safe journey. The 'grey' part refers to the grayish-green color of this plant's small, soft leaves, which helps distinguish it from its brighter green speedwell cousins.
description: Grey field-speedwell is a tiny, creeping annual weed that forms low mats close to the ground. This European native produces minuscule blue flowers with white centers that are barely bigger than a pinhead. The entire plant rarely grows taller than your thumb, with small, oval leaves that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch. It's easily overlooked unless you're looking closely at disturbed soil or garden beds.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pale blue flowers with white centers, only about 2-3mm across with four petals - so small you might need to get down on hands and knees to see them clearly

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves with a distinctive grayish-green color and soft, slightly fuzzy texture when you rub them between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground, rarely getting taller than 2-3 inches with stems that feel tender and break easily

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces tiny heart-shaped seed capsules that split open to release minute brown seeds

habitat: Look for grey field-speedwell in disturbed soils like garden beds, agricultural fields, and waste areas throughout New England. It thrives in cultivated ground and areas where the soil has been turned over, often appearing as a weedy groundcover in vegetable gardens and flower beds. This introduced species prefers nutrient-rich, moist soils in full sun to partial shade.

seasonality.spring: Flowers begin appearing in early spring and the soft, grayish leaves emerge as small rosettes close to the ground.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with tiny blue flowers visible throughout summer, though you'll need to look very closely to spot them.
seasonality.fall: Continues flowering into fall until frost kills the annual plants, with seed capsules developing and releasing seeds.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to germinate the following spring.

funFact: Despite being one of New England's most overlooked wildflowers, grey field-speedwell is actually blooming right under your feet in many gardens - its flowers are so tiny that most people walk right over entire carpets of them without ever noticing they're there!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small speedwells, especially bird's-eye speedwell which has similar tiny blue flowers. The key difference is the leaf color - grey field-speedwell has distinctly grayish-green leaves while bird's-eye speedwell has bright green leaves. Remember: 'grey' speedwell has grey-green leaves!
contextualKnowledge: This is one of New England's rarest speedwells with only 7 recorded observations, making it a special find for plant enthusiasts. Many speedwells were historically used in folk medicine, and the genus name Veronica comes from Saint Veronica, though the connection to these tiny weeds remains a botanical mystery.
compareHints: Grey field-speedwell stands out from its speedwell relatives primarily by its grayish leaf color and extremely small size. While corn speedwell and bird's-eye speedwell also grow low to the ground, they have brighter green foliage. Heath speedwell and thyme-leaved speedwell are perennials that form more substantial mats, whereas grey field-speedwell is an annual that appears more delicate and ephemeral.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's speedwells, heath speedwell is unique for its distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth habit and very fuzzy stems and leaves.
Among New England's speedwells, thyme-leaved speedwell is unique in its strongly creeping, mat-forming habit - most other speedwells grow more upright.
Among the speedwells, germander speedwell stands out for having the brightest blue flowers and the most prominent flower stalks that clearly rise above the foliage.
Among the speedwells, corn speedwell is distinguished by its fuzzy leaves and very small size - it's one of the tiniest in the genus.
Among the speedwells, marsh speedwell is distinctive for its wetland habitat and very narrow leaves.
Bird's-eye speedwell stands out from its many speedwell relatives by having the brightest, most intensely blue flowers with the most prominent dark radiating lines.
Among the many speedwells in New England, American brooklime is the water-lover of the group.
Among New England's many speedwell species, purslane speedwell stands out for its highly variable leaf shapes on a single plant and its preference for the most disturbed habitats.
Unlike the upright thyme-leaved speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell, slender speedwell stays flat to the ground with its characteristic thread-thin stems.

Long-leaved Speedwell towers over most other New England speedwells - while species like Thyme-leaved Speedwell hug the ground and Germander Speedwell stays low in lawns, this species stands tall with substantial flower spikes.
Unlike most other New England speedwells that are annual weeds or die back completely in winter, creeping speedwell is a true perennial that forms permanent mats.

Among New England speedwells, broadleaf speedwell stands out for its relatively large, oval leaves and dense flower spikes - most other speedwells have much smaller, narrower leaves and more open flower arrangements.
Among New England's many speedwells, blue water-speedwell is unique in its aquatic lifestyle - while American brooklime also likes wet areas, it grows taller and has larger flowers.
Among New England's speedwells, ivy-leaved speedwell is easily distinguished by its distinctive lobed leaves that look like tiny ivy leaves.
Unlike its lowland speedwell relatives that grow in fields and gardens, American alpine speedwell is the mountain specialist of the family.
Spiked speedwell towers over its New England speedwell relatives, most of which are small, creeping, or prostrate plants with much smaller flower clusters.
Among the many speedwells in New England, Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell stands out for its distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves - most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves.
Among the speedwells, chain speedwell is unique for its strong preference for aquatic habitats and its creeping, often floating growth habit.
